t: The organised campaign for women’s votes, usually dated from the Seneca Falls Convention in New York in 1848, won its first national victory in New Zealand in 1893.
Suffragists used petitions, conventions, lobbying and marches; in Britain the militant suffragettes smashed windows, set fires and went on hunger strike in prison.
Much of Europe and North America gave women the vote around the First World War, but many women of colour and colonial subjects waited decades longer.
dyk: In Finland’s first election with women voters, in 1907, nineteen women won seats in the new parliament, the first women elected to a national legislature anywhere in the world.
ev: The Seneca Falls Convention in New York adopts the Declaration of Sentiments, which demands the vote for women
Wyoming Territory gives women the vote; the American movement splits into two rival national associations
New Zealand becomes the first self-governing country to give all adult women the vote in national elections
Emmeline Pankhurst founds the Women’s Social and Political Union in Manchester
Finland gives women both the vote and the right to stand for parliament, the first European country to do so
Britain gives the vote to women over 30 who meet a property qualification
The Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution is ratified
Swiss men vote to give women the vote in federal elections

f.where: Arose in the United States and Britain; first won in New Zealand and Australia, then spread through Europe, Latin America, Asia and Africa
f.period: 1848–1971, from the Seneca Falls Convention to Switzerland’s federal vote; the first national victory in New Zealand in 1893 and a wave of victories in Europe and North America in 1906–1920
f.figures: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, Kate Sheppard, Millicent Garrett Fawcett, Emmeline Pankhurst, Carrie Chapman Catt
f.outcome: Votes for women in national elections across the world; equal suffrage made an international standard by the Convention on the Political Rights of Women (1952)
